topic: Socio-cultural Issues in Physical Activity and Sport
subject: pe

moments.title: Roger Bannister breaks 4 minutes
moments.body: On 6 May 1954 at Iffley Road track, Oxford, medical student Bannister runs a mile in 3:59.4, paced by Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. The crowd of 3,000 hears the first announcement break off after 'three' — Norris McWhirter's deliberate pause to maximise drama. 46 days later, Australian John Landy lowers the record to 3:58.0.

quote.attrib: Norris McWhirter announcing Bannister's time, 6 May 1954

moments.takeaway: Bannister was a part-time runner with a hospital job. The 'impossible' record was broken by an amateur preparing in lunch breaks.

moments.title: Usain Bolt's 9.58s 100m
moments.body: On 16 August 2009 Bolt runs the 100m in 9.58 seconds — the largest single-race improvement in 30 years (0.11s off his own world record). His top speed exceeds 44 km/h. The record still stands.
moments.takeaway: Athletics records typically fall by hundredths; Bolt rewrote sprinting by tenths. Genetic variation, training, technology and stadium conditions all combined.

now.title: Athletics today
now.body: World Athletics (formerly IAAF) governs the sport. Eliud Kipchoge's sub-2-hour marathon (1:59:40, Vienna 2019, unofficial) was the 4-minute-mile equivalent of its era — assisted by pacers and shoe technology. Nike Vaporfly and successor shoes triggered controversies and rule changes (40mm sole limit).
now.open_questions: How should performance-enhancing technology be regulated? The line between innovation and unfair advantage moves over time.

reflection: Bannister became a neurologist and dismissed his mile as far less important than his medical work. The athlete he was for one afternoon overshadowed the doctor he was for 50 years.
